alt: Flower structure compared: the bean flower has a standard, wings, a keel enclosing the stamens with anthers and a pistil with stigma, style and an ovary of ovules, so it self-pollinates inside the keel; the maize plant has a tassel with anthers at the top and a cob with silks lower down, and wind carries pollen from tassels to the silks of other plants.
caption: Figure: the bean flower (self-pollinated) and the male and female flowers of maize (wind cross-pollinated)

alt: Longitudinal sections of a bean seed and a maize grain: the bean has a testa, hilum, micropyle, two food-storing cotyledons, plumule and radicle and no endosperm; the maize grain has a pericarp fused with the testa, a large starchy endosperm, a scutellum, a plumule in a coleoptile and a radicle in a coleorhiza.
caption: Figure: sections of a bean seed and a maize grain with their parts labelled

alt: Bar chart of the broiler batch: costs of chicks US$90, feed US$224 (the largest), vaccines US$8, electricity US$25, transport US$15 and litter US$6 add up to US$368, against income of US$611 from 94 birds, a profit of US$243.
caption: Figure: the costs of the broiler batch against its income (profit US$243)

alt: Side view of the bull's reproductive system: testis and epididymis inside the scrotum, the vas deferens carrying sperm up to the urethra near the bladder, accessory glands adding fluid to make semen, and the penis with its S-shaped sigmoid flexure inside the sheath.
caption: Figure: the reproductive system of the bull (schematic)

alt: Bar showing a cow's calving interval of 368 days: 85 days from calving to conception plus a 283-day gestation, which overshoots the 365-day target; to calve every year she must conceive within 82 days of calving (365 minus 283).
caption: Figure: the calving interval of Tendai's cow (85 + 283 = 368 days) against the 365-day target

alt: Cross-section of two contour ridges on a slope: each has a channel dug on the uphill side that catches runoff and a grassed bank of the excavated soil thrown downhill; the ridges are 1.0 m apart in height (vertical interval) and 25 m apart horizontally on a 4% slope.
caption: Figure: a cross-section of two contour ridges, with the vertical interval and horizontal spacing

alt: Plan of a 200 m field on a 4% slope: a storm drain along the top keeps runoff from higher land out, eight contour ridges 25 m apart (1.0 m vertical interval divided by 4% slope) cross the slope with a very gentle fall to a grass waterway on the right that leads to the stream.
caption: Figure: laying out eight contour ridges 25 m apart below a storm drain, draining to a grass waterway

alt: Front view of the cow's reproductive tract: two ovaries, each with an oviduct where fertilisation takes place, leading to two uterine horns that join in the uterine body, then the thick-walled cervix, the vagina and the vulva.
caption: Figure: the reproductive system of the cow (schematic)

alt: Cross-section of a small earth dam: a wall much wider at the base than the top with a clay core, a cut-off trench of compacted clay down to the impermeable base, stone pitching on the upstream face, grass on the downstream face, freeboard above the full water level, and pressure arrows that get longer with depth because water pressure doubles when the depth doubles.
caption: Figure: the parts of a small earth dam and why the wall is thickest at the base

alt: Section through a hen's egg: shell with pores and cuticle, two shell membranes, an air cell at the broad end, thick and thin albumen, chalazae holding the yolk in the centre, the vitelline membrane, the yolk and the germinal disc; for a 60 g egg the shell is 6 g (10%), albumen 36 g (60%) and yolk 18 g (30%).
caption: Figure: the parts of an egg, and the shell, albumen and yolk shares of a 60 g egg

alt: Germination in three stages: the bean (epigeal) forms a hypocotyl hook that pulls its cotyledons above the soil surface, while the maize grain (hypogeal) stays below ground and its coleoptile pushes the first leaves up through the soil.
caption: Figure: epigeal germination in the bean and hypogeal germination in maize

alt: Plan of Farai's 40 ha farm (800 m by 500 m): a 3 ha woodlot on the northern ridge, four arable fields of 3.75 ha forming a 15 ha block, the homestead beside the main road on the east boundary with the pig and poultry houses to its west (downwind), the garden and orchard near the borehole, four paddocks on the lower slope and a fenced stream and vlei on the south boundary.
caption: Figure: a farm layout for the 40 ha plot, with the arable block divided into four fields of 3.75 ha

alt: Side view of a cattle fence: four strands of barbed wire, closer together near the ground, line posts 10 m apart with three droppers in each span, and straining posts at the ends held up by a box brace (left) and a diagonal stay to a block in the ground (right).
caption: Figure: a wire fence with line posts, droppers and two kinds of anchor on the straining posts

alt: Bar chart for maize at US$0.30 per kg: the value of the extra yield from bags 1 to 5 of fertiliser is US$180, 150, 105, 45 and 15 against a cost of US$35 a bag, so the 4th bag still pays but the 5th loses US$20, making 4 bags per hectare the most profitable rate.
caption: Figure: the value of the extra maize from each bag of fertiliser against the US$35 cost of a bag

alt: Plan views of field drainage layouts: a herringbone pattern with side drains joining a central main drain at an angle, and a gridiron pattern of parallel drains running into a main drain that leads to the outlet.
caption: Figure: herringbone and gridiron patterns for field drains (plan view)

alt: Four-course rotation on 12 ha: four fields of 3 ha carry maize, soya beans, sunflower and grass ley, shown for year 1 and year 2 as each crop moves one field along; on every field the order is maize, soya beans, sunflower, ley, and the maize field gets 30 t of manure a year.
caption: Figure: a four-course rotation on four 3 ha fields, years 1 and 2, and the order of crops on each field

alt: Timeline of the Jersey heifer's heats: standing heat seen on 3 March 2026, then expected heats 21 days later on 24 March and again on 14 April, each heat lasting less than a day.
caption: Figure: predicting the next heats of the heifer, 21 days apart (3 March, 24 March, 14 April 2026)

alt: Hen's reproductive tract in order: the left ovary with many yolks, the infundibulum (15 minutes, fertilisation), the magnum (3 hours, albumen), the isthmus (1 1/4 hours, shell membranes), the uterus or shell gland (about 20 hours, shell) and the vagina to the cloaca; the times add to about 24.5 hours, which is why a layer lays about one egg a day.
caption: Figure: the hen's oviduct, what each part adds and the time an egg spends in it

alt: Bar chart for 2,000 square metres needing 30 mm in the root zone: the crop needs 60,000 litres, drip irrigation at 90% efficiency must supply 66,667 litres and furrow irrigation at 60% efficiency must supply 100,000 litres, so drip saves 33,333 litres each time.
caption: Figure: water to supply for a 60,000 L crop need, drip (90%) against furrow (60%)

alt: Three irrigation methods in cross-section: furrow irrigation runs water along furrows between ridges (efficiency about 50 to 70%), a sprinkler sprays water over the crop from a riser on a lateral pipe (about 70 to 80%), and drip irrigation drips water at each plant so only the root zone is wetted (about 90%).
caption: Figure: furrow, sprinkler and drip irrigation compared, with typical efficiencies

alt: Cross-section of a dicotyledonous leaf from top to bottom: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll full of chloroplasts, spongy mesophyll with air spaces and a vein with xylem above phloem, then the lower epidermis with a stoma between two guard cells that lets carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
caption: Figure: a section through a leaf, from the waxy cuticle to the lower epidermis

alt: Bar split of the 2 ha maize gross output of US$2,610 (9 t at US$290): variable costs of US$1,050 (seed 110, basal fertiliser 330, top dressing 250, chemicals 90, hired labour 160, transport 70, bags 40) leave a gross margin of US$1,560, which is US$780 per hectare.
caption: Figure: where the US$2,610 gross output of 2 ha of maize goes, leaving a gross margin of US$1,560

alt: Side view of an ox-drawn mouldboard plough from front to back: trek chain, hake on the beam, wheel, coulter, frog carrying the share, mouldboard and landside with its heel, and the handles; the share cuts the furrow slice, the mouldboard turns it and the landside keeps the plough straight.
caption: Figure: the parts of a mouldboard plough, front to back

alt: Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen gas is fixed by lightning, Rhizobium, free-living bacteria and industry; ammonification by decomposers makes ammonium, Nitrosomonas makes nitrite and Nitrobacter makes nitrate, which roots take up into plants and animals; denitrification returns nitrate to nitrogen gas in waterlogged soil.
caption: Figure: the nitrogen cycle, with the organism or agent at each step and the losses in red

alt: Plan of the 200 m by 150 m paddock fence with a post every 10 m: 70 posts in a closed loop with four corner straining posts, 2,800 m of wire (700 m times 4 strands, which is 5.6 rolls so 6 are bought), 210 droppers and a materials cost of US$878.
caption: Figure: the 70 posts of a closed paddock fence, and the quantities and cost worked out in the text

alt: Life cycles compared: the fall armyworm has complete metamorphosis (egg mass on a leaf, larva that eats the funnel and does the damage, pupa resting in the soil, adult moth) while the locust has incomplete metamorphosis (egg pod in the soil, wingless nymph or hopper, adult), with no pupa and damage by both nymphs and adults.
caption: Figure: complete metamorphosis (fall armyworm) and incomplete metamorphosis (locust)

alt: Flow diagrams of non-ruminant digestion: the pig has mouth, oesophagus, one simple stomach, small intestine, small caecum, colon and rectum; the fowl has beak, oesophagus, crop for storing food, proventriculus with acid, gizzard for grinding, small intestine, two caeca and a cloaca.
caption: Figure: the digestive tract of the pig (one stomach) and the fowl (crop, proventriculus and gizzard)

alt: Two genetic diagrams for polled (P) and horned (p) cattle: Pp crossed with Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp and pp, a 3 polled to 1 horned ratio; a test cross of Pp with pp gives two Pp and two pp, a 1 polled to 1 horned ratio.
caption: Figure: Punnett squares for the F1 x F1 cross (3:1) and the test cross (1:1) in polled and horned cattle

alt: Bar chart of potometer rates from the bean shoot: 3 mm per minute in still air and shade, 6 in still air and bright light, 11 with a fan in bright light and 2 with a plastic bag over the shoot; light doubles the rate, wind raises it a further 83.3% and high humidity cuts it.
caption: Figure: potometer rates (distance moved in 5 minutes divided by 5) under four conditions

alt: Bar chart of where 250 cubic metres of rain from a 25 mm storm on 1 hectare goes: runoff 50 m3 (20%), infiltration 175 m3 (70%) and evaporation 25 m3 (10%), which add up to 250 m3.
caption: Figure: where the 250 m3 of rain from a 25 mm storm on 1 ha goes

alt: Graphs from the garden table: total product rises to a maximum of 1,900 kg at 5 workers then falls to 1,850 kg at 6; marginal product peaks at 600 kg for the 2nd worker, falls to 100 kg for the 5th and becomes negative (minus 50 kg) for the 6th; average product peaks at 500 kg per worker at 2 to 3 workers; stages I, II and III are marked.
caption: Figure: total, marginal and average product for 0 to 6 workers on one hectare

alt: Two panels showing osmosis at a root hair: in normal dilute soil water, water moves into the root hair cell whose sap is more concentrated; with fertiliser placed against the roots the soil solution becomes more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moves out of the root hair and the seedling wilts and looks scorched.
caption: Figure: water moves into a root hair from dilute soil water but out of it when fertiliser makes the soil solution stronger

alt: Cross-sections side by side: a dicotyledonous root with a star of xylem in the centre and phloem between its arms, a dicotyledonous stem with vascular bundles in a ring (phloem outside, xylem inside, pith in the middle), and a maize stem with its bundles scattered.
caption: Figure: where xylem and phloem lie in a dicot root, a dicot stem and a maize stem

alt: Ruminant stomach of an adult cow drawn with circle areas in proportion to capacity: the rumen holds 160 L (80%), reticulum 10 L (5%), omasum 15 L (7.5%) and abomasum 15 L (7.5%); food passes from oesophagus to rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum and then the small intestine, and cud returns to the mouth.
caption: Figure: the four compartments of a cow's stomach, drawn in proportion to their capacity

alt: Soil profile of Pit 1: dark crumbly topsoil (A horizon) 25 cm deep over red-brown subsoil (B horizon) down to 120 cm, then weathered rock fragments (C horizon) above bedrock; the topsoil holds the humus and feeding roots and the red-brown subsoil shows good drainage.
caption: Figure: the soil profile of Pit 1 with its three horizons and their depths

alt: Soil textural triangle with the jar-test soil plotted: 60% sand, 25% silt and 15% clay meet inside the sandy loam region; clay is read across on horizontal lines, sand along lines sloping up to the left, silt along lines sloping up to the right.
caption: Figure: the textural triangle, with Rudo's jar-test soil (60% sand, 25% silt, 15% clay) in the sandy loam region

alt: Partial budget for 1 ha of soya beans instead of maize: gains are extra income US$1,056 plus maize costs saved US$525, a total of US$1,581; losses are extra soya costs US$410 plus maize income lost US$1,305, a total of US$1,715; the net change is minus US$134 so the change would lower profit.
caption: Figure: gains and losses of replacing 1 ha of maize by soya beans (net change minus US$134)

alt: Section of a cylindrical storage tank with inside radius 1.5 m and water depth 2 m on a raised stand, showing the screened inlet, cover, overflow pipe, outlet tap above the floor and scour valve at the bottom; its volume is 14.137 cubic metres or 14,137 litres, which lasts 30 cows using 1,500 litres a day for 9.4 days.
caption: Figure: the features of a storage tank and the capacity calculation from the worked example

alt: Bar chart of a 60 mm storm: 12 mm runs off, 6 mm evaporates, 22 mm is stored in the soil to field capacity and 20 mm drains below the root zone, and 12 + 6 + 22 + 20 equals the 60 mm of rain.
caption: Figure: where the 60 mm of rain goes (12 + 6 + 22 + 20 = 60 mm)

alt: Bar chart per crate of tomatoes: the farm gate price is US$4.00; in Harare the US$7.00 price is reduced by US$1.20 transport and a US$0.30 market fee to a net US$5.50, which is US$1.50 more per crate and US$90 more for 60 crates.
caption: Figure: farm gate against the net town price for a crate of tomatoes

alt: Demand and supply graph for crates of tomatoes: demand falls from 900 crates at US$2 to 100 at US$10 while supply rises from 100 to 900; they meet at the equilibrium of US$6 and 500 crates; at US$8 supply exceeds demand by 400 crates (surplus) and at US$4 demand exceeds supply by 400 crates (shortage).
caption: Figure: the tomato market schedule plotted: equilibrium at US$6 and 500 crates

alt: Water cycle on a farm landscape: 1 evaporation from sea and dam, 2 transpiration from crops, 3 condensation into cloud, 4 precipitation, 5 interception on leaves, 6 infiltration and percolation to the water table, 7 surface runoff to the dam, 8 groundwater flow through the aquifer towards the sea.
caption: Figure: the water cycle, numbered in the same order as the stages in the text
